bull_bear.body:
- Established capabilities in woven apparel manufacturing, retained through the restructuring of the platform
- Broad customer base rebuilt after the exit of VF Corporation through an extensive customer-development programme in FY2024-25
- Longstanding customer relationships that management chose to protect by absorbing part of the US tariff impact
- Natural hedge on foreign exchange, with imports almost 40%-50% of exports, alongside a stated policy of systematically hedging long- and short-term currency exposures
- Harmonious industrial relations at all units with no man-days lost to strike or lock-out, and a stated 'Injury Free' / 'Zero Environment Incident' safety vision
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- US tariff and trade-policy exposure — A significant portion of the customer base rebuilt after VF Corporation's exit is exposed to the US market. Additional tariffs on India-origin supplies directly hit the commercial economics of several programmes; customers sought substantial price reductions and the Company absorbed part of the impact through discounts and price reductions aggregating approximately C 18.70 crore in FY2025-26. Management states tariff volatility remains an important risk for an export-oriented business and that trade policy can move pricing, margins and customer sourcing decisions quickly.
- Customer concentration — Explicitly listed among continuing risks. The business was severely disrupted by the exit of a single customer, VF Corporation, at the end of calendar 2023, which destroyed significant volume and capacity utilisation and forced a multi-year rebuild.
- Intense pricing competition in apparel exports — Listed among continuing risks; the post-VF portfolio was larger and more fragmented with highly price-sensitive programmes that raised operating complexity without generating contribution sufficient to support the existing manufacturing and fixed-cost structure.
- Fixed-cost / capacity-versus-profitable-business mismatch — Management flags the ability to maintain the appropriate balance between manufacturing capacity and available profitable business as a continuing risk. The Avadi facility closure and right-sizing cost approximately C 6.25 crore in one-time charges, and the rationalisation continues into FY2026-27.
- Foreign exchange risk — Activities expose the Company to foreign exchange risk from foreign currency transactions, primarily USD and EURO. Mitigated by a policy of systematically hedging long- and short-term exposures plus a natural hedge from imports of almost 40%-50% of exports; the Company discloses net USD exposure and a sensitivity of profit after tax to exchange-rate moves.
- Working-capital and liquidity risk — Working-capital requirements are listed among continuing risks, and changes in commercial and shipment arrangements increased the cost and working-capital burden borne by the Company. Liquidity risk management depends on maintaining sufficient cash and committed credit facilities to meet obligations when due; the current ratio remained at 1.00 during FY2025-26.
- Credit risk on unsecured trade receivables — The Company faces credit risk from cash and bank deposits and from unsecured trade receivables — the primary source of credit risk being that receivables are unsecured; impairment is assessed individually for major clients, and the Company states that as at 31st March 2026 it had no significant credit risk.
- Raw-material, labour and logistics cost inflation, and rising compliance/sustainability requirements — Listed among apparel-industry risks alongside geopolitical disruptions and fluctuations in global demand; increasing quality, sustainability and compliance requirements add cost and execution burden. Mitigation is stated as focus on operational efficiency, cost management, quality, timely delivery and strong customer relationships.

outlook.body:
- Align capacity, customers and costs around commercially sustainable business rather than chasing volume or utilisation alone
- Continue capacity rationalisation — the additional Avadi facility was closed (process initiated February 2025, completed August 2025) as it was no longer commercially sustainable after VF Corporation's exit
- Consolidate operations in FY2026-27 by relocating activities from leased premises into Company-owned facilities to reduce the fixed-cost base
- Align manpower, administrative overheads and other operating costs with the consolidated manufacturing structure
- Apply a more selective approach to customer and product development, reviewing each programme for contribution, operating complexity, working-capital requirement and long-term relationship potential
- Deepen engagement with existing customers by broadening the range of products and categories offered, alongside acquiring new customers
- Evaluate product and market opportunities arising from India's expanding network of free trade agreements
- Retain established capabilities in woven apparel manufacturing while building a more balanced portfolio of customers, products and markets
- Systematically hedge long-term and short-term foreign exchange exposures in line with the hedging policy, supported by a natural hedge from imports of almost 40%-50% of exports
- Restore sustainable profitability while retaining capabilities and customer relationships needed for future growth
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY2025-26 was a year of capacity REDUCTION rather than expansion. The Company continued its capacity-rationalisation programme: the additional manufacturing facility at Avadi, originally established to support the requirements of the erstwhile VF business, was judged no longer commercially sustainable after VF Corporation's exit, and its closure — initiated in February 2025 — was completed in August 2025, with the closure and associated right-sizing exercise involving one-time costs of approximately C 6.25 crore. The stated objective of the programme is to move away from carrying capacity in anticipation of volume towards an operating structure supported by economically sustainable business. Into FY2026-27 the capacity-optimisation programme has continued, with a further consolidation of operations achieved by relocating activities from leased premises into Company-owned facilities, intended to reduce the fixed-cost base and align manufacturing capability and infrastructure with current business requirements; manpower, administrative overheads and other operating costs are being aligned with the consolidated structure. Management says the Company will continue to evaluate opportunities for expansion as the business environment improves, while maintaining discipline over capacity, costs and working-capital deployment; no named expansion project, commissioning timeline or capex quantum is disclosed. The Capital Commitments note states that capital expenditure contracted for at the end of the reporting period but not recognised as liabilities is nil ('-') for both years presented.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- US tariff policy is the dominant swing factor: additional tariffs on India-origin supplies hit the commercial economics of several programmes, and customers sought substantial price reductions to offset the duties
- The Company chose to absorb part of the tariff impact — tariff-related discounts and price reductions aggregated approximately C 18.70 crore in FY2025-26 — to protect strategically important customer relationships
- Changes in global trade arrangements and the continued development of free trade agreements may improve India's competitiveness in certain markets and product categories, creating an opportunity to pursue new markets and broaden the product portfolio
- A larger and more fragmented, price-sensitive customer portfolio raised operating complexity without generating contribution sufficient to cover the existing manufacturing and fixed-cost structure — hence the shift to quality over volume
- Costs of rationalising the manufacturing platform continued to weigh on profitability; the Avadi closure and right-sizing involved one-time costs of approximately C 6.25 crore
- Trade policy can move pricing, margins and customer sourcing decisions quickly, so tariff volatility remains an important risk for an export-oriented business
- Working-capital burden rose in certain cases from changes in commercial and shipment arrangements
- Management frames the restructuring as building a more efficient operating platform from which to progressively rebuild sustainable and profitable growth, not merely shrinking the business

- Domestic (sales to customers located in India)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- US tariff policy is the dominant swing factor: additional tariffs on India-origin supplies hit the commercial economics of several programmes, and customers sought substantial price reductions to offset the duties
- The Company chose to absorb part of the tariff impact — tariff-related discounts and price reductions aggregated approximately C 18.70 crore in FY2025-26 — to protect strategically important customer relationships
- Changes in global trade arrangements and the continued development of free trade agreements may improve India's competitiveness in certain markets and product categories, creating an opportunity to pursue new markets and broaden the product portfolio
- A larger and more fragmented, price-sensitive customer portfolio raised operating complexity without generating contribution sufficient to cover the existing manufacturing and fixed-cost structure — hence the shift to quality over volume
- Costs of rationalising the manufacturing platform continued to weigh on profitability; the Avadi closure and right-sizing involved one-time costs of approximately C 6.25 crore
- Trade policy can move pricing, margins and customer sourcing decisions quickly, so tariff volatility remains an important risk for an export-oriented business
- Working-capital burden rose in certain cases from changes in commercial and shipment arrangements
- Management frames the restructuring as building a more efficient operating platform from which to progressively rebuild sustainable and profitable growth, not merely shrinking the business

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Align capacity, customers and costs around commercially sustainable business rather than chasing volume or utilisation alone
- Continue capacity rationalisation — the additional Avadi facility was closed (process initiated February 2025, completed August 2025) as it was no longer commercially sustainable after VF Corporation's exit
- Consolidate operations in FY2026-27 by relocating activities from leased premises into Company-owned facilities to reduce the fixed-cost base
- Align manpower, administrative overheads and other operating costs with the consolidated manufacturing structure
- Apply a more selective approach to customer and product development, reviewing each programme for contribution, operating complexity, working-capital requirement and long-term relationship potential
- Deepen engagement with existing customers by broadening the range of products and categories offered, alongside acquiring new customers
- Evaluate product and market opportunities arising from India's expanding network of free trade agreements
- Retain established capabilities in woven apparel manufacturing while building a more balanced portfolio of customers, products and markets
- Systematically hedge long-term and short-term foreign exchange exposures in line with the hedging policy, supported by a natural hedge from imports of almost 40%-50% of exports
- Restore sustainable profitability while retaining capabilities and customer relationships needed for future growth

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY2025-26 was a year of capacity REDUCTION rather than expansion. The Company continued its capacity-rationalisation programme: the additional manufacturing facility at Avadi, originally established to support the requirements of the erstwhile VF business, was judged no longer commercially sustainable after VF Corporation's exit, and its closure — initiated in February 2025 — was completed in August 2025, with the closure and associated right-sizing exercise involving one-time costs of approximately C 6.25 crore. The stated objective of the programme is to move away from carrying capacity in anticipation of volume towards an operating structure supported by economically sustainable business. Into FY2026-27 the capacity-optimisation programme has continued, with a further consolidation of operations achieved by relocating activities from leased premises into Company-owned facilities, intended to reduce the fixed-cost base and align manufacturing capability and infrastructure with current business requirements; manpower, administrative overheads and other operating costs are being aligned with the consolidated structure. Management says the Company will continue to evaluate opportunities for expansion as the business environment improves, while maintaining discipline over capacity, costs and working-capital deployment; no named expansion project, commissioning timeline or capex quantum is disclosed. The Capital Commitments note states that capital expenditure contracted for at the end of the reporting period but not recognised as liabilities is nil ('-') for both years presented.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Established capabilities in woven apparel manufacturing, retained through the restructuring of the platform
- Broad customer base rebuilt after the exit of VF Corporation through an extensive customer-development programme in FY2024-25
- Longstanding customer relationships that management chose to protect by absorbing part of the US tariff impact
- Natural hedge on foreign exchange, with imports almost 40%-50% of exports, alongside a stated policy of systematically hedging long- and short-term currency exposures
- Harmonious industrial relations at all units with no man-days lost to strike or lock-out, and a stated 'Injury Free' / 'Zero Environment Incident' safety vision

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- US tariff and trade-policy exposure — A significant portion of the customer base rebuilt after VF Corporation's exit is exposed to the US market. Additional tariffs on India-origin supplies directly hit the commercial economics of several programmes; customers sought substantial price reductions and the Company absorbed part of the impact through discounts and price reductions aggregating approximately C 18.70 crore in FY2025-26. Management states tariff volatility remains an important risk for an export-oriented business and that trade policy can move pricing, margins and customer sourcing decisions quickly.
- Customer concentration — Explicitly listed among continuing risks. The business was severely disrupted by the exit of a single customer, VF Corporation, at the end of calendar 2023, which destroyed significant volume and capacity utilisation and forced a multi-year rebuild.
- Intense pricing competition in apparel exports — Listed among continuing risks; the post-VF portfolio was larger and more fragmented with highly price-sensitive programmes that raised operating complexity without generating contribution sufficient to support the existing manufacturing and fixed-cost structure.
- Fixed-cost / capacity-versus-profitable-business mismatch — Management flags the ability to maintain the appropriate balance between manufacturing capacity and available profitable business as a continuing risk. The Avadi facility closure and right-sizing cost approximately C 6.25 crore in one-time charges, and the rationalisation continues into FY2026-27.
- Foreign exchange risk — Activities expose the Company to foreign exchange risk from foreign currency transactions, primarily USD and EURO. Mitigated by a policy of systematically hedging long- and short-term exposures plus a natural hedge from imports of almost 40%-50% of exports; the Company discloses net USD exposure and a sensitivity of profit after tax to exchange-rate moves.
- Working-capital and liquidity risk — Working-capital requirements are listed among continuing risks, and changes in commercial and shipment arrangements increased the cost and working-capital burden borne by the Company. Liquidity risk management depends on maintaining sufficient cash and committed credit facilities to meet obligations when due; the current ratio remained at 1.00 during FY2025-26.
- Credit risk on unsecured trade receivables — The Company faces credit risk from cash and bank deposits and from unsecured trade receivables — the primary source of credit risk being that receivables are unsecured; impairment is assessed individually for major clients, and the Company states that as at 31st March 2026 it had no significant credit risk.
- Raw-material, labour and logistics cost inflation, and rising compliance/sustainability requirements — Listed among apparel-industry risks alongside geopolitical disruptions and fluctuations in global demand; increasing quality, sustainability and compliance requirements add cost and execution burden. Mitigation is stated as focus on operational efficiency, cost management, quality, timely delivery and strong customer relationships.
